speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The SIP assisted eligible micro and small companies (MSCs) facing financial difficulties by helping them restructure their debts, rehabilitate their business or wind up via a simpler, faster and lower cost insolvency process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The SIP was scoped to assist MSCs, because MSCs form a significant proportion of the enterprise ecosystem in Singapore and are the lifeblood of our economy and our communities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 2022, for instance, small enterprises accounted for about 94% of Singapore's enterprise landscape.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The purpose underpinning the SIP was, thus, to provide a simplified process that was tailor-made for MSCs – simpler, faster and more cost-effective.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have found in the time that we have introduced the SIP, that it was, by and large, useful in assisting MSCs in severe financial distress.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For simplified winding up, the completion of cases was done with an average of nine months and some as quickly as a few months.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This compares very favourably to a typical process, which could take anywhere between three to four years, especially where there is a longer tail of transactions and contracts to resolve.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This shorter process allowed non-viable companies to be liquidated quickly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The expedited process saves time and costs and lessens the impact on the principals behind the business while preserving the value of the insolvency estate for distribution to creditors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For simplified debt restructuring, there were fewer cases compared to simplified winding up.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A successful case was the restructuring of Axis Group Asia Private Limited.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This was done with Court sanction in under six months, which was a very short period of time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With the success of the SIP, this Bill now seeks to introduce a refined SIP, one which I shall call the SIP 2.0, to make it a permanent feature of our corporate debt restructuring and insolvency regime in the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018 (IRDA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As there is merit in making the SIP permanent as part of the insolvency and restructuring ecosystem, we explored further, over the course of the last couple of months, how the current SIP could be suitably modified to allow companies that are not MSCs to also benefit from it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We consulted with public agencies and stakeholders from the private sector and the industry was generally supportive of having the SIP as a permanent programme and provided helpful feedback for us to refine the framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have taken this on board, where possible, to improve the current SIP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SIP 2.0 seeks to provide a simpler and more cost-effective insolvency process to benefit more companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill will, therefore, modify two existing processes under the SIP, namely the Simplified Debt Restructuring Programme (SDRP); and the Simplified Winding Up Programme (SWUP).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Unlike the current SIP, the processes in SIP 2.0 will be fully administered by licensed insolvency practitioners in the private sector who are experienced and have the relevant expertise.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This approach, Members may know, is consistent with other corporate insolvency processes, such as the Court-ordered winding up and creditors' voluntary winding up, which are administered by private liquidators who are also licensed insolvency practitioners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members will also recall how our companies' winding up regime became fully administered by private liquidators when the IRDA came into force in July 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The approach for the SIP is, thus, consistent with existing debt restructuring and insolvency processes where the private sector currently already takes the lead.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, let me take Members through the key changes to the SIP, which this Bill proposes to implement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, the eligibility criteria apply to both the SDRP as well as the SWUP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will make it much easier for companies that are not MSCs to also benefit from the SIP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Under the SDRP, a company will draw up a debt restructuring proposal for its creditors, which provides for a compromise or, otherwise, an arrangement to resolve its debts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill will modify the existing SDRP in several key aspects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To begin with, we will reduce the number of supporting documents accompanying the SDRP application to require only key supporting documents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A Restructuring Adviser, who is a licensed insolvency practitioner appointed by the company to advise the company in matters relating to its entry into the SDRP, will assess whether the company reaches or matches the requirements for the SDRP and request for further documents from the company, if necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Companies failing to successfully complete the SDRP, including the current SDRP, will be barred for five years before they can, again, apply for the SDRP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This serves to protect the interests of creditors and prevents errant companies from abusing the SDRP by making repeated entry applications to avoid its obligations to creditors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To give Members some colour into the second criterion, one such circumstance is prescribed in the amended section 72F(3)(h), which is when the company is unlikely to be able to formulate a proposed compromise with its creditors or to obtain the agreement of two-thirds majority by value of its creditors to the proposed compromise or arrangement, within the moratorium period after the company's entry into the SDRP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, you get 30 plus 30, a maximum of 60 days for a moratorium within which to frame the restructuring proposal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This, Sir, balances the interests of the various stakeholders by providing reasonable breathing room to the company to propose a debt restructuring plan whilst, at the same time, protecting the interests of the creditors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members will know that during the moratorium period, there will be no enforcement against the corporate entity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Once the company has entered into the SDRP, its Restructuring Adviser will provide assistance in drawing up the debt restructuring proposal to its creditors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The notice to summon the meeting must contain such information as is set out in section 72M(3) and I will just quickly summarise what they are.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It must include details of the proposal, a statement of the effects of the proposal on creditors' rights, a comparison of what the creditors would receive in the proposal and the most likely scenario if the compromise or arrangement pursuant to the proposal does not become binding on the company and its creditors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It must also contain information on the Restructuring Adviser's remuneration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This notice must be given to every creditor of the company.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In practice, as Members would know how such restructuring takes place is that the Restructuring Adviser would have engaged in informal discussions and talks with the creditors prior to the meeting.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And depending on the outcome of these discussions, the Restructuring Adviser would, by then, already have a keen sense of how the creditors will expect to receive the proposal and whether any changes might need to be made, while the creditors would also have heard about the proposal's terms before formally receiving the notice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Nevertheless, we believe that this is essential as the notice is a formal measure to provide substantive fairness to all creditors so that they are apprised of the terms of the proposal and know ahead of the meeting what they are going in for, prior to the meeting.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This threshold remains unchanged from the existing programme.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There will be one voting class consisting of all unsecured creditors, ordinary and preferential, if applicable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Secured creditors will only be bound by the proposal if the value of the security interest is less than the value of the secured creditor's admissible debts or claims, only to the extent of the difference between the values, and that means the undersecured portion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, for Members' clarity, the difference between the value of the security for a secured creditor and the unsecured portion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, the differential is the only portion that will apply.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The secured creditors will also be bound by the proposal if the value of the secured interest is equal to or more than the value of the secured creditor's admissible debts or claims, but only to the extent that the creditor consents to be bound.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, in some cases, a creditor might well have sufficient security but might decide that the restructuring proposal makes sense and wants to participate and take part, in which case, the creditor can support the restructuring arrangement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This means, therefore, that a secured creditor is free to realise or deal with his security interest unless he has voted in favour of the proposal and consented to be bound and the proposal's terms prevent him from realising or otherwise dealing with his security interest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A creditor who is bound by the proposal can apply to Court to object to the proposal on specified grounds under section 72N(3), where there is a material procedural irregularity in relation to the meeting of the company and its creditors to approve the proposal or in relation to the approval of the creditors at the meeting; for the proposal to be fair and equitable to all creditors bound by it, a substitution or splitting of classification of creditors is necessary; or the approved proposal is contrary to the interests of the creditors of the company as a whole.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Court hearing this application may make any order it thinks fit, including revoking or suspending the compromise or arrangement of the proposal and giving directions to the Restructuring Adviser, including a direction to put to the creditors for consideration any modifications to the compromise or arrangement, except, the material commercial terms of the proposal may not be modified.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will now touch on the key proposals for the SWUP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This Bill modifies the existing SWUP in the following key aspects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This new feature simplifies the application process and encourages non-viable companies to be wound up instead of remaining dormant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There may be situations where members of the company are uncontactable and the company is, thereby, unable to pass a special resolution to enter into the SWUP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: All these are factors which speak to the company's dormancy and we believe it is in the interest to have these companies wound up rather than remain on the books.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the current SWUP, there are four platforms on which notices are published: the Official Receiver's website; the Government's e-Gazette; the local newspaper; and the Registrar of Companies' BizFile under the Accounting, Corporate and Regulatory Authority or ACRA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 38 modifies section 180 and section 210 of the IRDA to streamline the final or early dissolution processes of a company, respectively, by requiring only one lodgement with ACRA to effect the dissolution of the company.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Additionally, where a liquidator requires funding from creditors to conduct investigations to recover assets but no such funding is forthcoming, the liquidator may complete the simplified winding up of the company and dissolve the company without taking further investigative steps.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This ensures that unviable companies, which will have no other assets and, sometimes, no other identifiable members, can be liquidated and dissolved efficiently without having to restart or unnecessarily protract the liquidation process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The rest of the SIP, as I said at the outset, will remain unchanged.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This Bill aims to modify the SIP and make it a permanent feature of our insolvency regime in the IRDA modifying the existing processes in the current SIP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will make the SIP permanent, or as I call it, SIP 2.0.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One which is simpler, more cost-effective and will also facilitate better access to insolvency processes and, with these changes, benefit a larger group of companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I seek to move.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This programme has been an important lifeline to micro and small companies facing financial difficulties, helping them to restructure or wind up efficiently.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, I would like to raise some concerns on behalf of Singaporean business owners, creditors and employees who may be affected by these changes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Although the inclusion of larger companies in the SIP is well-intentioned, it can potentially disadvantage creditors and employees, particularly when the winding up process is expedited.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For small creditors, this could mean reduced chances of recovering debts owed to them.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Employees may also be left in limbo if unpaid salaries and benefits are deprioritised.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry clarify how these stakeholders will be protected, especially when the larger companies avail themselves of the scheme?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Local newspapers remain a trusted medium for many Singaporeans, particularly small and medium enterprise (SME) owners and sole proprietors, who may not closely monitor the digital channels.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I appeal to the Ministry to retain this requirement or ensure alternative notification methods are as effective in reaching out to all the stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While protecting creditors' rights is essential, some businesses may require additional time to sort out their affairs, particularly for SMEs managing limited resources.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, as we extend its accessibility, we must ensure that safeguards remain robust and that the interests of all stakeholders, creditors, employees and business owners, are adequately addressed.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Ministry to take these considerations into account.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Bill that is currently being debated seeks to render permanent the centerpiece of the previous amendments, the SIP.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Along the way, it further streamlines two parts of the SIP, namely the SDRP and SWUP.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As Minister Edwin Tong has already elaborated, these include a number of appealing and commonsensical refinements, such as shortening the moratorium period in SDRP, limiting the eligibility criteria to just one for SWUP and reducing the number of required supporting documents for both processes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Today, in addition to touching on three elements in the present Bill, I will also address two broader concerns that align with the spirit of the issue: first, how much bang for the buck we are truly gaining by further simplifying corporate bankruptcy in this manner; and second, whether there is a pressing need to also consider whether individual bankruptcy proceedings can be simplified more as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On the present Bill, I will note, first, that clause 38 will now require the notification of the dissolution of the firm to be published on the designated website only, without also doing so in the Government's e-Gazette or newspapers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The permanent record will also be available on ACRA's Bizfile.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This move is, as I understand it, an effort to reduce the costs of the new SWUP.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I understand the motivation to reduce costs, especially for newsprint, I wonder why the publication on the e-Gazette, which should be the most complete official journal of the country's public and legal notices, is precluded.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, notices there are already electronic in nature and a half-page entry costs a little more than $100.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If this is prohibitive, perhaps, a waiver or fee reduction can be considered for such instances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The justification appears to be a desire to strengthen creditor rights.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The natural question here is, if this "30 days" is reasonable and sufficiently balances creditor protection with debtor difficulties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would the Government be willing to share with this House the historical mean and median times for restructuring plans to be completed in Singapore?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If it does not have this information, how was the decision to reduce the moratorium from 90 to 30 days ultimately arrived at?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is a seemingly simple but important step to ensure that restructuring can proceed expeditiously without one or two low-key creditors preventing an efficient resolution of the debt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This so-called holdout problem has been an affliction, especially in sovereign debt restructuring instances and has led to significant problems due to the presence of so-called vulture investors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This move essentially embeds a collective action clause as a means of ensuring post-default resolution and is one way to usher negotiations or renegotiations to a close.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I do not necessarily disagree with the approach here, I would like to know if the two-thirds majority will be weighted by each creditor's exposure, since I believe that this would be fairer than a one-creditor-one-vote system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would also add that another way to try to bring about the outcome is through exit consents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These allow the majority to alter the non-financial terms of the debt in a way that would make the debt shares of holdouts effectively worthless.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This strategy may be even more preferable insofar as ensuring that even initial holdouts ultimately deliver a consensual, even if acquiescent, vote, rather than one where a supermajority alone may ram through their preferred outcome.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my earlier speech on the 2020 IRDA amendments, I had expressed my support for less onerous, appropriately designed resolution procedures since doing so would have helped bolster a more entrepreneurial mindset, especially in a knowledge and information-driven economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This was especially important then, when the shadow of COVID-19 and the associated spike in business failures may have led to heightened risk aversion among small business owners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet over the intervening four years, the record on the actual usage of SIP does not appear to suggest that the issues addressed by SIP were major binding constraints.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Admittedly, the SIP applies only to small and micro enterprises.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But given how around two-thirds of companies in Singapore are actually small firms and how small firms are, typically, much more likely to fail, this does not seem to be too poor an estimate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If indeed the need for simplified insolvency is so pressing, why would the take-up rate be so limited?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: According to the World Bank, the strength of Singapore's insolvency framework scored 74.3 out of 100 in 2020, placing it 27th in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this may suggest ample room for improvement, the reported weaknesses had little to do with speedy bankruptcy resolution or high costs, both of which our nation ranked among the best worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather, they relate more to the management of debtors' assets, limited creditor participation and the poor involvement of creditors in re-organisation proceedings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Future revisions of the corporate bankruptcy framework may wish to bear these lessons in mind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, any reduced costs of doing business for our small and medium enterprises are welcome.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This begs the question, then, of whether the resolution regime for individual bankruptcies can be further expedited and simplified, much like what we are doing here for companies in this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Doing so may even improve our business climate, since the nature of entrepreneurship today is that many individuals take on personal debt to pursue their dreams of starting their own companies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be fair, there have been some advances on that front.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Debt Repayment Scheme (DRS), modelled after Chapter 13 of the United States (US) Bankruptcy Code, offers a debt resolution alternative that is more flexible and forgiving than traditional bankruptcy, at least for debts below a certain threshold.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But after more than a decade and a half, DRS appears to be fraying at the edges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As my Sengkang colleague Mr Louis Chua recently pointed out, third-party consultants are being engaged to help with the administration of the programme and the fees they charge may be a concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) does not regulate third-party debt consultancies or the fees that they charge, which potentially allows such consultancies to take advantage of distressed Singaporean borrowers, thereby worsening their debt burden at a time where they least need it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is undeniable that there should be some nominal fee for the administrative costs incurred by the Official Assignee (OA).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The 1.5% collection and 3% distribution fees by OA may be seen as punitive, especially if the debt amount turns out to be rather significant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The DRS hearings also, currently, exempt creditors from attendance, which may introduce inadvertent delays in the process of discharge, especially in instances where the repayment schedule also needs to be re-negotiated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In addition, Singapore remains somewhat of an outlier among advanced economies where there is no automatic discharge from bankruptcy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The United Kingdom (UK) wrote this out in its Insolvency Act 1986 while Hong Kong did the same at the end of the 1990s; Germany and France followed a few years after and even neighbouring Malaysia started in 2017.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, even the elapsed duration before a discharge may even be considered by OA here, is a long three years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Contrast this to Canada, where the duration for automatic discharge is nine months for first timers with no surplus income, and 24 months for second timers; or the UK, where bankrupts only have to wait for a year after the order is first issued; or the US, where debts under Chapter 7 bankruptcy occurs four months after filing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This was last raised in 2015 from $10,000.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, taking inflation into account means that that would be equivalent to about $18,000 in today's dollars.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While we are here debating a permanent extension of the pandemic-era accommodations for corporate bankruptcy, I would urge the Ministry to also do the same for individual bankruptcy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The possibility that we face a tide of even more personal bankruptcies in the year ahead is very real.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rising cost of living have placed immense pressure on many households.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Retrenchment spiked in 2023 and are likely to remain high for 2024.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Interest rates on debt worldwide, including Singapore, have remained stubbornly high, even after the more recent rate cut cycle by the US Federal Reserve.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This portends, yet, more challenges for Singaporeans who are struggling under the burden of debt.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Over the years, this programme has proven its value, offering businesses a faster, simpler and more cost-effective way to restructure the debts or wind-up operations.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: With a focus on efficiency and fairness, the proposed changes are designed to provide businesses with the tools they need to navigate financial distress while preserving value for creditors.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This simplified framework will be of great help to SMEs in some financial stress, while supporting others to wind down with dignity.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This amendment seeks to do more than just extend the programme.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill's provisions outline the eligibility criteria for businesses seeking to enter the simplified debt restructuring programme.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I would seek the Minister's views on whether companies with complex ownership structures qualify for the programme, such as those with multiple layers of ownership or significant cross-border operations.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs with international operations face unique challenges, especially dealing with creditors across jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Will the SIP framework accommodate the specific complexities these businesses face, especially regarding validating the debts or assets in multiple countries?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Number three, when a business faces financial distress due to factors beyond its control, such as global supply chain disruptions or international trade restrictions, will such companies be considered eligible for SIP assistance, even if their financial difficulties stem from external, non-operational factors?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Number four, given the current economic climate of relatively high inflation and interest rates, can the Minister please clarify, if the SIP's entry requirements will be sufficiently flexible to accommodate businesses facing these external challenges?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Specifically, will the criteria consider the impact of these economic pressures on a company's financial position, ensuring that otherwise viable businesses are not unfairly excluded from accessing this crucial support?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This question is particularly pertinent, given the findings of the recent Singapore Business Federation's National Business Survey 2024/2025.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These statistics underscore the need for flexibility in our insolvency framework.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Number five, one of the key elements of the proposed amendments is the role of the Restructuring Adviser in guiding businesses through the simplified debt restructuring process.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Given the importance of this role, does the Bill include safeguards to prevent conflicts of interest?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Will there be clear guidelines for how Restructuring Advisers are selected and will there be a mechanism for businesses to challenge or request a change of advisors if they feel that the current advisors are not acting in their best interest?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Number six, I now turn to the compliance and penalties under clause 6, section 72E(4).

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed amendments also introduce new compliance and penalty provisions.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While these provisions will help ensure that businesses follow the proper procedures, I seek the Minister's clarification on what constitutes materially false or misleading statements under the Bill and how these will be assessed.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: It would also be helpful to understand whether businesses will have the opportunity to rectify any misstatements before penalties are imposed.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Number seven, will there be specific thresholds or guidelines for penalties and will there be proportionality between the nature of the offence and the consequences for the company involved?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Number eight, an important aspect of this Bill is the support for SMEs with limited access to restructuring professionals under its general provisions.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Will there be financial assistance or subsidies for smaller businesses to help them engage professional advisors, such as restructuring specialists or legal counsel, during the insolvency process?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Number nine, how can the Government partner with industry bodies or trade associations to create awareness and provide training for SMEs on navigating the insolvency process?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Minister consider setting up a dedicated SME advisory panel to provide ongoing feedback and suggest improvements?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Number 10, will there be any provisions to protect employees and other stakeholders, such as suppliers, who may be affected by a company's closure?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Since SMEs often rely on close personal relationships with local suppliers and employees, these parties must be treated fairly during a simplified winding process.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While this is a welcome development, how will the Government ensure that SMEs, particularly those without significant digital infrastructure, be able to adapt to this new approach?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Will assistance or training be available for businesses that may face challenges in transitioning to these digital systems?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: More broadly, what comprehensive plans are in place to educate our SME community about the SIP and its benefits, particularly on the new changes?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I thought I would start with a few broad overarching points which underpin the proposed amendments – overarching in the sense that these are the purposes and the broad principles that underpin why we have decided to introduce SIP 2.0.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They also answer some of the points that Members have raised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, I think we all agree, it is not economically viable or desirable for companies that are not operating, dormant for a period of time and not financially sustainable, to remain on the books.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, in some ways, there will be individual personalities behind these companies as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the simplified process allows them to get out of a business that has failed, through perhaps no fault of theirs, in a straightforward manner and get on with a different business; an exit that is fair to all creditors, and find the business transactions under a different model and perhaps, one which may be more viable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it also helps the individuals behind each of these corporate entities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, we all agree that, in reality, the practical challenges and realities facing smaller companies in financial distress would be very different from the larger companies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Here, I want to emphasise a few points.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, we are dealing with a scenario which is a small subset in terms of the type of cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Although I said, at the start, that MSCs form the bulk of our enterprise landscape, but the type of cases that we are dealing with is a subset of the broader ones.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, my first point to many of the issues raised by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim as well as by Mr Neil Parekh and Mr Don Wee, is that the parties have a choice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, they should assess for themselves how suitable their case is for a SIP 2.0 process and decide whether they fall under this framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Otherwise, the entire framework in the IRDA is completely available to any of these companies as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is not as if they are locked into or pigeonholed into having to select SIP 2.0, if they qualify as an MSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is the first point I would make.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The numbers speak to the cases that have come under SIP 1.0 in the immediate post-COVID-19 enactment of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But as I said, this is a choice that we are offering as an add-on to a corporate entity to decide whether they fit within this profile and, if so, whether they want to avail themselves of a shorter, more simplified process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Effectively, it is giving more options rather than taking away or requiring some companies to fit within this framework without having a choice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The third point I would make is that we see, therefore, value in having insolvency processes that are in the context of these cases, simpler, more straightforward, more streamlined, easier to get entry into, not so document-intensive and allows the companies to decide: I fit within this framework, let us get onto this quickly so that I can simplify, reduce cost as well as use up less time to exit a failed business.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we envisage that SIP 2.0 will have this impact and overall, in these cases, translate into better returns for creditors, which is one of the key aims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Because sometimes, and Members might know that I have spent some time in practice doing restructuring, we see a very viable, very good restructuring plan, but it takes time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And at the end of the day, a lot of the cost would eat up the balance assets of the company after the restructuring is completed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We hope that in these cases, for the MSCs in particular, that when they avail themselves of this framework, there will be bigger savings in time and costs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With this in mind, let me address some of the specific points that Mr Wee, Assoc Prof Lim as well as Mr Parekh had raised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I said, I thank Members for the carefully considered speeches.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Mr Wee's point, the proposed framework seeks to balance the various considerations, providing a streamlined insolvency process and also, we understand, the interests and expectations of the stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think it is important, while this is streamlined, for Members to know that we are not compromising on rights that creditors will have and should have in any insolvency.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As mentioned in my opening speech, public agencies and private sector stakeholders have also been consulted widely as part of the design process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will continue to engage them on an ongoing basis to ensure that this framework that we have proposed in SIP 2.0 remains accessible and evolves with the times to keep up with the needs of corporate entities in financial distress.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: By taking into account industry feedback and streamlining the requirements and processes, we have also sought to reduce the cost and time burdens on companies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Broadly speaking, and I say this in the context of the fact that we have amended the requirements from just an MSC alone to looking at the nature of the insolvency itself, I would say that larger companies with a more sophisticated set-up and larger debt sizes where you have complexity in disputes across different jurisdictions would typically not be suitable for such a simplified process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This applies to both simplified as well as non-simplified processes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Unsecured debts rank lower in terms of priority.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This was the position when we first introduced the SIP as well and will continue to be so in SIP 2.0.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What is envisaged to change under SIP 2.0, however, is that we believe, as I mentioned earlier, the remaining pie for distribution is expected to be larger.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is because the costs and expenses of the liquidation should reduce.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As such, rather than employees or creditors having to feel disadvantaged from this, if this is made out, then in fact, the distribution at the end of the process would be expected to be higher.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, various safeguards exist to prevent potential abuse as the directors' statement will facilitate more efficient entry into simplified winding up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, the nominated liquidator has the ultimate responsibility for assessing whether this company satisfies the eligibility requirements or not.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In particular, if there is complexity or if there is a suggestion that there is wrongdoing or fraud, the company may be transited into a non-simplified insolvency process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If such fraud or wrongdoing is discovered only after the company has entered into simplified winding up, in other words, midstream and whilst the process has already started, then the liquidator can likewise transit the company into a non-simplified process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it facilitates the transfer between the schemes quite seamlessly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Wee, Assoc Prof Lim and I think Mr Parekh also talked about notifications.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Only one notice must also be published in at least one local English daily newspaper, namely, the notice of acceptance into the scheme itself under the current section 250J(c) of the IRDA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Assoc Prof Lim's point about notices, and I think he made an appeal whether we could consider other forms, at the end of the day, it is not our intention to deprive creditors and other stakeholders of notice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We felt that this would be the best balance between costs, time taken and the burden on the companies seeking the simplified process and notification.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In our feedback sessions with the industry, we felt that they were already familiar with the current process – publication on the website and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Having this as the sole mode of publication will reduce costs and not at the same time cause undue concern to stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Assoc Prof Lim's point, I will make two further responses.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I said, it is not the intention to deprive proper parties with stakeholder interest or any interest from knowing that this has commenced or has started.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will evaluate the efficacy of the notice and make changes where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The other, of course, as I said in my opening speech, if there is a process of procedural irregularity or defect, the party affected by that under the SDRP says, "Look, I wasn't aware there was a notice and now I find myself bound by the SDRP", that individual creditor can apply to Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One of the grounds of relief, as I stated, is process irregularity, which includes notice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, let me deal with the length of the moratorium period.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are simplified, straightforward and ought to be dealt with quickly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I also mentioned in my speech that by and large, in many of these processes, one expects – in fact, it happens in practice – the Restructuring Adviser to already engage the parties, the stakeholders, the creditors, in particular, on the proposed plan and the scheme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Once that happens, you will trigger the process, you start the 30 days for you to work out the details, you might get a further extension if you are not able to satisfy that and then within this framework, you must find a solution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We believe this to be a proper balance between the fact that you are dealing with a $2-million debt, probably in as much as these are MSCs, you probably also find that the countervailing parties, the creditors themselves, are probably also MSCs or perhaps individuals and there is an interest in ensuring that their rights are also not compromised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One further point to Assoc Prof Lim is that this period will be prescribed in subsidiary legislation as set out in clause 20 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if we find, as this evolves that it is actually insufficient time, we can make adjustments along the way quite easily.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think I have addressed some of them, so I will deal with the rest of Mr Parekh's considerations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The key consideration is that the insolvency should be straightforward and not something that is mired in complexity or disputes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Depending on the circumstances, some types of companies that Mr Parekh has mentioned may be eligible for SIP 2.0.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For more complicated cases – cross-border elements, disputes that are contentious, fraud, wrongdoing, fraud with disputes between parties, maybe challenges between creditors for priority and so on – then the non-simplified process is still available and in fact, would be more suitable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Mr Parekh's point on conflict of interest, Restructuring Advisers are professionals and they must deal with this issue in the course of their work, as they do all the time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, as Mr Parekh knows, it is one topic that comes up from time to time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The introduction of SIP 2.0 does not take away that obligation to evaluate their personal position relative to any conflict of interest that they might have.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are bound by their licensing conditions and regulated by their respective accountancy professional bodies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think we all know that if they do not act professionally, complaints can be made and the Official Receiver or the Licensing Officer or the professional bodies can look into that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, the law provides for the company to appoint Restructuring Advisers and does not restrict the companies to only one such appointment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In appropriate cases, the company may appoint a new Adviser but obviously, the company will have to balance that against the increase in time and cost that might bring about.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, Mr Parekh asked about the scope of the offences in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Like those in other laws, they will be determined by the Courts based on established principles.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This includes the new section 72E(4), which is materially identical to the existing section 72E(5).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are not changing the threshold or, in fact, the substantive ingredients behind the offences proposed in section 72E(4).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Based on the evidence and circumstances of the case, the Courts will determine whether a specific statement is "false or misleading in a material particular".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We put that framework and formula in – and I think Mr Parekh asked to give examples – because what is false and misleading in the context of a statement may well differ from case to case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They may differ in the context of one type of business or another or one form of representation or another.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We wanted to keep it situational and contextual, so that the Court has the ability to evaluate, based holistically on the circumstances of each case, whether it is false or misleading in that particular circumstance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court will also determine the applicable penalties to be imposed in the context of sentencing discretion, which is not unusual; while the Government will consider the circumstances of cases, including rectification by companies, before deciding whether to prosecute.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On Mr Parekh's concerns about digital filings and notifications, SIP 2.0 does not introduce any new processes that are not already part of the current SIP.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned earlier, publishing notifications on the Official Receiver's website already exists under the current SIP.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While this process will be enhanced for the convenience of Restructuring Advisers and liquidators under SIP 2.0, significant digital infrastructure will not be required for that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Before I conclude, let me also make two assurances.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned to Assoc Prof Lim, we will also continue to monitor the efficacy of the thresholds and the framework that we put in and make adjustments where necessary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I want to assure Assoc Prof Lim that this is something that my Ministry has already started looking into.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We understand the points that he has made.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have in fact started work on this, consulted, internally, some stakeholders before going public subsequently.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is an issue that we are studying and we will come back to this House in due course.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Besides benefiting stakeholders of the affected companies, this, we believe, will support the broader economy by facilitating the reallocation of resources towards more productive businesses.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I seek to move.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just a quick follow-up on the issue of educational efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am wondering if there will be additional guidance or advisory by MinLaw that would at least usher MSCs that qualify for SIP to pursue this route when shareholders make the difficult decision to restructure or wind up?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Or is this left to corporate bankruptcy lawyers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I ask because, of course, not to deprive legal practitioners such as Minister Tong in his previous life, but MSCs do not always have access to such expensive legal counsel.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I am not sure if it is expensive legal counsel, but legal counsel.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will also, of course, work with the insolvency professionals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They would be the ones who perform the role of the Restructuring Advisers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is not as if it is a completely new creature.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But we will take further steps to enhance it, should there be a need to.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The citation year "2024" will be changed to "2025", as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.
